content: The right-hand rule is a widely used mnemonic in mathematics and physics to clarify the conventions for representing vectors in three-dimensional space. This rule was introduced by the British physicist Ambrose Fleming in the early 1900s. When dealing with three vectors that must be mutually perpendicular, there are two possible orientations. To eliminate ambiguity in mathematical expressions, a specific convention must be chosen. Variations of the right-hand rule exist depending on the context, but they all adhere to the principle of selecting a consistent convention. One application of the right-hand rule involves determining the direction associated with an ordered pair of vectors. For example, when performing an operation on two vectors, (a) and (b), that results in a third vector, (c), which is perpendicular to both (a) and (b), the right-hand rule provides a method to resolve the ambiguity of (c)'s direction. A common example of this is the vector cross product. To apply the rule, one must position the thumb, index finger, and middle finger of the right hand at right angles to each other. The thumb represents the direction of (a), the index finger represents (b), and the middle finger points in the direction of (c). Another form of the right-hand rule is used to assign a vector to the rotation of a body, a magnetic field, or a fluid. In this context, the fingers of the right hand are curled to follow the curvature and direction of the rotation or field, while the thumb indicates the direction of the associated vector. The first form of the right-hand rule is extensively used in physics to determine the direction of the cross product of two vectors. This has numerous applications, including the following: Determining the angular velocity of a rotating object and the rotational velocity of any point on the object. Relating torque, the force causing it, and the position of the point of application of the force. Understanding the relationship between a magnetic field, the position where it is measured, and the electric current (or change in electric flux) that generates it. Analyzing the magnetic field in a coil of wire and the electric current flowing through the wire. Calculating the force exerted by a magnetic field on an object, the magnetic field itself, and the velocity of the object. Describing the vorticity at a point in the flow field of a fluid. Determining the induced current resulting from motion in a magnetic field, as described by Fleming's right-hand rule. Fleming's left-hand rule, on the other hand, is used to find the direction of the thrust on a conductor carrying a current in a magnetic field. In some cases, it may be necessary to use the opposite convention, creating a left-handed triad instead of a right-handed one. This is particularly relevant for left-handed materials, which exhibit unique properties such as a negative refractive index. In such materials, the direction of wave propagation is reversed compared to the right-hand rule. De Graaf's adaptation of Fleming's left-hand rule and the right-hand rule is known as the FBI rule. This rule replaces thrust with (F) (Lorentz force), (B) (magnetic field direction), and (I) (current). The FBI rule is easily remembered by U.S. citizens due to its association with the Federal Bureau of Investigation.
